title: "Ex Vivo and In Situ Hypothermic Hepatic Resection"

## Introduction to Complex Liver Surgery

- Liver surgery techniques and imaging are constantly evolving
- Allows ever more detailed planning of surgical strategy
- Development of living-donor liver transplantation (LDLT) created comfort with vascular and biliary reconstruction techniques
- These techniques are now applied to complex nontransplant liver surgery

## The Challenge of Vascular Reconstruction

- Principal difficulty: necessary period of hepatic ischemia
- Liver tolerates moderate ischemia surprisingly well
- Hepatic inflow occlusion (Pringle maneuver) often used during parenchymal transection
- Combined with low central venous pressure (CVP), allows relatively bloodless transection

## Ischemic Preconditioning

- Intermittent hepatic inflow occlusion protects the liver from subsequent ischemic injury
- Technique: Pringle maneuver for 10 minutes, then reperfusion for at least 10 minutes
- Mechanisms not fully elucidated
- Even longer periods of continuous ischemia are relatively well tolerated

## Tolerance to Warm Ischemia

- Normal liver can tolerate 60 minutes or more of continuous inflow occlusion
- Patients with cirrhosis, biliary obstruction, or prolonged chemotherapy tolerate significantly less
- Older patients may also have reduced tolerance
- Risk of irreversible damage increases with prolonged continuous ischemia

## When Standard Techniques Are Insufficient

- Vascular reconstruction may require bloodless field longer than acceptable
- Tumors involving retrohepatic IVC or hepatic veins (HVs) may require total vascular isolation
- Total vascular isolation may increase ischemic injury more than inflow occlusion alone
- Backward diffusion of HV blood may attenuate ischemic injury

## Planning Complex Resections

- Most complex liver tumor resections can be done without ex vivo or in situ cold perfusion
- Tumors involving hilar vessels approached by temporary HA or PV occlusion
- HA and PV reconstructions may be done in sequence
- IVC involvement often approached with venous side-clamping or short-term total vascular isolation

## Truly Unresectable Lesions

- Minority of patients have lesions unresectable by conventional technique
- Cases where vascular reconstruction is complex and predicted to take considerable time
- Cases where transection is too dangerous to undertake in situ
- Classic example: centrally placed lesions involving all three main HVs, with or without retrohepatic IVC involvement

## Rationale for Hypothermic Perfusion Techniques

- Better access to the tumor
- Minimizing ischemic injury to future liver remnant using cold preservation
- Higher likelihood of complete R0 resection
- Theoretical concern: increased vascular and biliary complications due to re-anastomosis
- Good long-term survival rates observed in experienced centers

## Historical Development

- Experience limited to few high-volume liver surgery and transplantation centers
- Techniques mirror aspects of LDLT
- Importance of patient selection, preoperative evaluation, intraoperative decision making, and postoperative care
- Toronto Video Atlas of Surgery educational videos highlight key points

## History of Hypothermic Perfusion

- Fortner and colleagues (1974): first to describe hypothermic perfusion during liver resection
- Series of 29 patients
- Technical improvements over next two decades made hypothermic perfusion unnecessary in most cases
- Growing understanding of liver's ability to tolerate normothermic ischemia

## History of Liver Transplantation for Malignancy

- Liver transplantation applied to technically unresectable primary and secondary liver malignancy
- Results were dismal: rapid recurrence in new liver or elsewhere
- Especially poor for large unresectable primary tumors and metastatic lesions

## Development of Ex Vivo Resection

- Pichlmayr and associates (1988): developed hypothermic perfusion with ex vivo liver resection
- Liver completely removed from body
- Perfused with cold preservation solution on back table
- Resection performed in completely bloodless field
- Reconstruction of HV outflow under ideal conditions

## Evolution to In Situ and Ante Situm Techniques

- Ex vivo morbidity and mortality relatively high
- In situ and ante situm hypothermic perfusion techniques developed as alternatives
- Three techniques described: in situ hypothermic perfusion, ante situm hypothermic perfusion, ex vivo liver resection
- All mirror aspects of LDLT

## Comparison of the Three Techniques

- In situ and ante situm do not necessarily require HA and/or biliary reconstruction
- Risk for vascular and biliary complications may be lower compared with ex vivo
- Ex vivo provides outstanding exposure
- Ex vivo permits parenchymal hypothermic perfusion (unless HV outflow is clotted)

## In Situ Hypothermic Perfusion: Overview

- Aim: provide bloodless operative field with hypothermic cellular protection
- Permits prolonged and accurate dissection
- For resections necessitating vascular isolation or during vascular reconstruction
- Theoretically most straightforward, but IVC/HV exposure can be awkward

## Hannoun et al. 1993: Normothermic Ischemia Data

- Retrospective study of 34 patients with vascular occlusion exceeding 1 hour
- All patients had normal liver parenchyma
- Conclusion: continuous vascular occlusion safe on normal parenchyma up to 90 minutes
- Advocated hepatic vascular exclusion with in situ hypothermic perfusion when occlusion might exceed 120 minutes

## Hannoun et al. 1996: Diseased Liver Application

- Same group showed successful application in patients with underlying liver disease
- Cooling allows major hepatic resection using vascular exclusion longer than 1 hour
- No increased morbidity or mortality in this sensitive population

## Azoulay et al. 2005: Comparative Study

- Compared in situ hypothermic perfusion vs standard total vascular exclusion
- Assessed liver tolerance by AST/ALT peaks, bilirubin, PT, creatinine
- Hypothermic perfusion associated with better ischemia tolerance at any duration
- Better postoperative liver and renal function, lower morbidity for exclusions &gt;1 hour

## Predictive Factors for Longer Resection

- Azoulay et al. identified predictive factors for resection &gt;1 hour:
  - Size of tumor
  - Need for PV embolization
  - Planned vascular reconstruction
- These factors should guide decision for hypothermic perfusion

## Indications for In Situ Cold Perfusion

- Total vascular exclusion indicated for tumors involving or adjacent to IVC and/or HV confluence
- Original Fortner technique: mobilization for total vascular isolation
- Control of suprahepatic IVC, infrahepatic IVC, and portal structures
- Gastroduodenal artery isolated and cannulated
- PV cannulated via venotomy or branch of lobe to be resected

## Original In Situ Perfusion Technique

- Cannulae kept patent with slow Ringer's lactate infusion at room temperature
- Common HA and PV clamped proximal to cannulae
- Infrahepatic and suprahepatic IVC separately occluded
- Cavotomy made immediately inferior to liver for effluent drainage
- Ringer's lactate chilled to 4°C with 5mg/L heparin used for perfusion

## Role of Veno-Venous Bypass in In Situ Perfusion

- Standard use reduces time pressure and gut edema from prolonged portal clamping
- Most patients tolerate total vascular isolation without bypass
- Some series perform bypass routinely
- If used: sufficient PV length (3-4cm) dissected for perfusion and bypass cannulae

## Bypass Cannulation Techniques

- Portal clamp placed relatively superiorly on PV
- Bypass instituted below this clamp
- Portal cannula directed down toward SMV after PV division
- Alternative: divide anterior wall of PV and slide cannula down back wall
- Preferred method: temporary biologic graft onto anterior wall of SMV, then cannulate graft

## Modern In Situ Technique Without Bypass

- Advent of LDLT, anterior approach, and improved transection techniques
- Most parenchymal transection done without inflow occlusion
- Total vascular isolation applied only as transection nears completion
- Significantly shorter hepatic ischemia periods
- Generally does not require veno-venous bypass

## Portal Cannulation Options

- PV dissected to right and left branches
- Perfusion tubing placed into main PV
- Option 1: cannulate PV branch on opposite side of liver to be removed (Figure 124.2)
- Branch divided, maintaining portal flow to remnant but allowing cold perfusion access
- Option 2: anterior wall of main PV used for cannula insertion (Figure 124.3)

## Figure 124.2: Portal Cannulation in Branch

- Portal cannula inserted in right portal vein (RPV) branch
- Allows in situ perfusion of remaining segments II and III
- Case shown: infant undergoing resection for hepatoblastoma
- Cold perfusion allows IVC resection and repair of medial LHV

## Figure 124.3: Anterior Wall Cannulation

- Anterior wall of portal vein above portal clamp used for cannulation
- Allows cold perfusion without dividing portal branches
- Useful when preserving flow to entire remnant liver

## Staged Vascular Isolation

- As much parenchyma as possible divided under low CVP conditions
- Hepatic perfusion maintained until vessels requiring reconstruction must be divided
- Patient volume-loaded, inotropes started as necessary
- Clamps placed sequentially: infrahepatic IVC, PV, HA, suprahepatic IVC

## Partial Caval Clamping (Figure 124.4)

- If only HV requires reconstruction, caval flow can be maintained
- Clamp placed tangentially down onto IVC across HV orifice
- Partially occludes IVC
- Allows in situ perfusion without veno-venous bypass

## Figure 124.4: Tangential IVC Clamping

- Vascular clamp on IVC occluding implantation site of hepatic vein
- Maintains cava flow
- LHV and PV visible in operative field
- Technique reduces need for full bypass

## Figure 124.5: Continuous Cold Flushing

- Continuous cold flushing of remnant liver
- Allows resection and reconstruction of hepatic vasculature without time pressure
- Ice placed around liver for topical cooling
- Graft may be used for IVC reconstruction

## Reperfusion Sequence

- Before completing anastomoses: flush liver with cold 5% albumin
- Or flush with 300-400mL of PV blood with caval clamps still in place
- PV clamp reapplied, caval venotomy closed, all clamps removed
- Alternative warm-flush technique: vent initial 300-500mL blood through infrahepatic cava

## Results of In Situ Hypothermic Perfusion

- Azoulay et al. 2015: 77 liver resections with standard TVE and hypothermic portal perfusion
- 33 cases required vascular reconstruction
- 90-day mortality rate: 19.5%
- Independent predictors of mortality: age-adjusted CCI ≥3, tumor size ≥10cm, 50/50 criteria
- Overall 5-year survival: 30.4%

## Ante Situm Procedure: Introduction

- Least frequently used of the three techniques
- Used when resection of IVC and HVs expected to be difficult
- Improved access to HVs and IVC required
- Designed by Hannoun et al. (1991)

## Ante Situm Technique Concept

- Suprahepatic (and potentially infrahepatic) cava divided
- Liver rotated anteriorly
- Liver essentially exteriorized while connected only by hepatic pedicle
- Future remnant liver perfused via PV or HA
- Resection performed with involved HVs, remnant HVs reimplanted into vena cava

## Advantages of Ante Situm Approach

- Combines in situ hypothermic perfusion with separation of suprahepatic IVC
- Better mobilization of liver posteriorly by rotating anteriorly toward abdominal wall
- Used when combined IVC-HV reconstruction required
- Biliary and HA anastomoses NOT required
- Reduces ischemic time and potential complications

## Exposure for Ante Situm: Figure 124.6

- Phrenic veins divided bilaterally
- Suprahepatic IVC dissected away from diaphragm
- Provides adequate length for suprahepatic cava clamp
- Allows division with enough length for reanastomosis
- LHV visible in field

## Figure 124.7: Median Sternotomy Option

- Addition of median sternotomy provides excellent exposure
- Suprahepatic IVC (SIVC) and confluence of hepatic veins well visualized
- Right atrium (RA) accessible
- Sternotomy avoided when possible due to additional morbidity

## Intrapericardial Caval Control

- Control of intrapericardial cava allows upper clamp placement within pericardium
- Primary option for very large tumors
- Secondary option if technical difficulties with suprahepatic clamp
- Pericardium opened directly anterior to IVC

## Figure 124.8: Ante Situm Cold Perfusion

- Suprahepatic IVC divided
- Liver rotated forward
- Region of hepatic vein-IVC confluence better exposed
- Cold perfusion through portal vein
- Perfusate vented through divided suprahepatic IVC

## Figure 124.9: Veno-Venous Bypass in Ante Situm

- Bypass can be used during ante situm perfusion
- If more exposure required to retrohepatic IVC
- Infrahepatic IVC also divided
- Liver rotated completely up onto abdominal wall
- Greater access to posterior structures

## Figure 124.10: Clinical Example — Cholangiocarcinoma

- CT scan showing cholangiocarcinoma centered on all three hepatic veins
- Junction with IVC involved
- Right portal structures also involved
- Right trisegmentectomy with reconstruction of left hepatic vein indicated

## Figure 124.11: Ante Situm Operative View

- Parenchymal division along right trisegmentectomy plane
- Crossing into segments II and III superiorly
- Cannula in RPV stump for cold perfusion with UW solution
- Short segment of IVC at hepatic veins resected
- Liver rotated anteriorly
- IVC reconstructed end-to-end, LHV reimplanted above cava anastomosis

## Figure 124.12: Reimplanted Segments II and III

- Left hepatic duct reconstructed later using Roux-en-Y limb
- IVC anastomosis visible
- LHV anastomosis to reconstructed cava
- LPV and PV visible
- Demonstrates feasibility of complex reconstruction

## Ex Vivo Liver Resection: Introduction

- For tumors involving IVC and HVs requiring complex venous repair
- Combined complex HV and hilar involvement
- Severely compromised HV outflow
- Liver completely removed from patient
- Perfused with cold preservation solution on back table

## Indications for Ex Vivo Resection

- IVC-HV junction tumors requiring complex prolonged reconstruction
- Combined vascular involvement of HVs and hilar structures
- Involvement of all three HVs with venous outflow obstruction
- Attempts to mobilize liver off IVC would cause massive hemorrhage
- Acute Budd-Chiari picture

## Patient Selection: General Assessment

- Similar to liver transplantation evaluation
- Particular assessment of cardiac risk factors
- Detailed cardiovascular history: smoking, peripheral vascular disease, hypertension
- Functional stress test for patients &gt;50 or with cardiac abnormality
- Dobutamine stress echocardiogram if target heart rate achievement limited

## Contraindications to Ex Vivo Resection

- Significant cardiac abnormality
- Melendez et al. 2001: combination of factors leads to very high mortality:
  - Preoperative cholangitis
  - Elevated serum creatinine
  - Elevated serum bilirubin
  - &gt;3 liters operative blood loss
  - Vena cava resection
- Mild renal dysfunction (creatinine &gt;1.3 mg/dL) should be considered contraindication

## Preoperative Risk Factors

- Azoulay et al.: age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index ≥3
- Maximum tumor size ≥10 cm
- Number of comorbidities (CV, renal, pulmonary)
- Ex vivo resection only in otherwise healthy, well-selected patients

## Preoperative Imaging: CT and MRI

- Triphasic spiral CT with 3D reconstructions: standard
- Assess liver anatomy and tumor position
- CT chest and pelvis to rule out metastatic disease
- MRI with MR angiography and MR venography when all three HVs involved
- Invasive angiography almost always unnecessary with modern CT/MRI

## Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound and PET

- Contrast-enhanced ultrasound: dynamic view of tumor-HV/IVC relationship
- Particularly useful for estimating extent of vascular invasion
- PET scan considered for undetected extrahepatic disease
- Used in selected cases

## Remnant Liver Volume Assessment

- Standard: 25% of total liver volume (TLV) adequate for normal liver
- Patients with prolonged chemotherapy may require more (steatohepatitis)
- With cold preservation and reperfusion: additional ischemic injury
- Arbitrary cutoff: 40% of TLV for extended hepatectomy with complex vascular reconstruction
- May require preoperative portal vein embolization (PVE)

## 3D Imaging and Printed Models

- 3D printed liver models demonstrate anatomy with high accuracy
- Assist with preoperative planning
- May be used for simulation of surgical procedures
- Can reveal unusual anatomy making reconstruction unnecessary
- Or reveal anatomy requiring additional reconstruction

## Anesthesia: Multidisciplinary Team

- Optimized anesthetic management essential
- Circulation and hemodynamic stability
- Coagulation function
- Patient core temperature maintenance
- Rapidly growing field evolving from transplant surgery knowledge

## Hemodynamic Management

- Most challenging: PV and IVC occlusion, liver reperfusion
- Vasoactive agents used early to maintain stability
- Factors influencing hemodynamic changes:
  - Patient habitus
  - IVC collateral circulation
  - Sensitivity to vasoactive agents
- Test clamp before IVC and PV clamping essential

## Coagulation and Volume Management

- Sufficient blood products and albumin before vascular reconstruction
- Appropriate vasoactive doses before vena cava clamping
- Dose adjusted during reconstruction and before reperfusion
- Minimize crystalloid, use FFP or albumin for volume in anhepatic phase

## Temperature Management

- Major heat losses during:
  - Induction of anesthesia
  - Patient exposure and preparation
  - Anhepatic phase
  - Reperfusion
- Hypothermia causes platelet dysfunction, coagulopathy, cardiac conduction slowing, coronary vasospasm
- Forced-air warming, warmed fluids, heated humidifier, heated gel pads

## Monitoring and Bypass Access

- Swan-Ganz catheter for hemodynamic monitoring and PA blood temperature
- Veno-venous bypass access: percutaneous insertion techniques
- Low CVP maintained initially as for standard liver resections
- Percutaneous catheters in internal jugular/subclavian and infrarenal cava for bypass

## Anhepatic Phase Considerations

- Generally lasts 2 to 4 hours
- FFP or albumin for volume requirements
- Minimize crystalloid
- Glucose levels monitored; constant glucose infusion required
- PA blood temperature monitored continuously

## Reperfusion Temperature Management

- On reperfusion of cold autograft: PA blood temperature precipitously drops
- Manual compression of portal inflow when temperature &lt;35°C
- Portal occlusion for ~10 seconds allows PA temperature to rise to 36°C
- Repeated as necessary
- Avoids cardiac dysfunction from cold effluent

## Three Phases of Ex Vivo Resection

1. Assessment of resectability and removal of the liver
2. Liver resection and vascular reconstruction on the back table
3. Reimplantation of the liver autograft

## Phase 1: Assessment of Resectability

- Initial laparoscopy or limited abdominal incision for peritoneal disease
- Negative laparoscopy does not guarantee resectability
- Additional small lesions or peritoneal spread may be found
- Bilateral subcostal incision with or without midline extension preferred
- Midline sternotomy considered for hepatocaval confluence exposure

## Assessment of the Liver

- Assess for resectability
- Tumor involvement of HVs with or without IVC involvement
- Liver often congested from obstructed venous outflow
- Care during mobilization: small capsule breach causes torrential bleeding
- Venous congestion NOT a contraindication (resection relieves obstruction)

## Hilar Preparation: Step 1

- Arterial anatomy dissected
- Division site usually just above common HA-gastroduodenal artery junction
- Aberrant anatomy may require alternative site
- Preserve small arterial communications to biliary plate
- For perihilar cholangiocarcinoma: dissect far enough for tumor-free branch

## Hilar Preparation: Step 2

- PV identified, common bile duct (CBD) encircled without skeletonization
- Cholecystectomy performed
- CBD reflected off PV preserving blood supply
- Neural and lymphatic tissue around PV cleared
- PV and HA dissected and mobilized for individual clamping

## IVC Preparation: Infrahepatic

- Dissected down to level of renal veins and encircled
- Planned clamp placement immediately above renal veins
- Division may be more cephalad
- Right adrenal vein ligated and divided
- Small caudate veins divided if accessible

## Liver Mobilization

- Freed from surrounding attachments
- Challenging when liver congested from chronic venous obstruction
- If tumor infiltrating diaphragm: resect en bloc
- Large tumors may restrict rotation without undue tension
- Early decision for ex vivo approach before elevating liver off IVC

## Suprahepatic IVC Preparation

- Phrenic veins divided bilaterally
- Diaphragm dissected away from IVC
- Increased length of intra-abdominal IVC for clamping and reconstruction
- Pericardium opened directly anterior to IVC
- Intrapericardial IVC looped or midline sternotomy performed

## Pre-Removal Planning

- Clamp placement, transection lines, need for vascular conduits assessed
- HV branches reconstructed using HV or PV segments from resected side
- Autologous vein grafts: superficial femoral vein, proximal left renal vein, gonadal vein, saphenous vein
- Cryopreserved femoral or iliac vein grafts for long segments
- IVC replacement: 19-mm ringed PTFE (Gore-Tex) tube graft

## Figure 124.13: Veno-Venous Bypass Circuit

- Liver removed, patient on bypass
- A: Opening in pericardium for intrapericardial IVC control
- B: Vascular clamp on suprahepatic IVC
- C: Vascular clamp on hepatic artery
- D: Portal cannula in portal vein
- E: Vascular clamp on infrahepatic IVC

## Removal Sequence with Bypass

- Percutaneous access of internal jugular and femoral/infrarenal cava
- IVC clamped, caval bypass started
- PV clamped below bifurcation, portal cannula inserted toward SMV
- PV completely transected 1.5-2cm below bifurcation
- Portal flow added to bypass circuit
- CBD transected 1-1.5cm below bifurcation

## Figure 124.14: Temporary Portocaval Shunt

- Alternative to bypass in selected patients
- Prolonged anhepatic phase without veno-venous bypass
- Intrapericardial IVC encircled
- PC shunt constructed between PV and IVC
- CHA and GDA visible

## Alternative Without Bypass

- For complex HV involvement without IVC tumor involvement
- Liver completely mobilized off retrohepatic IVC
- Suspended only by HVs
- Hilar structures divided as for standard ex vivo
- Partial clamp across IVC occluding HV orifices but preserving cava flow
- Temporary portocaval shunt decompresses enteric circulation

## Hepatic Perfusion and Preservation

- Liver placed immediately in ice bath
- Perfused with preservation solution through PV
- UW or HTK solution used
- Initial 500-1000mL flushed through liver
- Effluent from IVC should be clear
- HA and biliary tree flushed with ~100mL additional solution
- Liver immersed in cold UW solution

## Cold Ischemic Time

- Exact accepted time to reimplantation not known
- Up to 4 hours associated with good outcomes
- Total cold ischemic time usually 2-4 hours
- Well within acceptable limits compared to split-liver or reduced-size allografts

## Back Table Resection: Overview

- Hilar structures dissected out and divided
- Care not to divide segmental arteries supplying remnant liver
- Main segmental PV divisions usually repairable and reconstructible
- Parenchymal transection: CUSA, water-jet, or sharp knife division
- No fear of blood loss during back table dissection

## Figure 124.15: Preoperative CT — Colorectal Metastasis

- Single colorectal metastasis involving all three hepatic veins
- RHV involvement visible
- Centrally placed tumor requiring complex outflow reconstruction

## Figure 124.16: Planned Hepatic Transection Line

- Dashed line shows planned transection
- Multiple hepatic vein branches require reconstruction
- Resection must preserve adequate remnant with viable venous drainage

## Figure 124.17: Back Table Transection Result

- Multiple branches of right hepatic vein requiring reconstruction
- Large segment VI branch entering middle hepatic vein also requires reconstruction
- Transection surface visible with multiple orifices

## Figure 124.18: Completed Back Table Transection

- Branches of RHV visible
- Segment 6 vein identified
- HA visible
- All visible vessels and ducts ligated or clipped to prevent bleeding

## Back Table Leak Testing

- Flush PV, HA, and CBD with cold preservation solution
- Identify leaks from cut surface
- Repair leaks before reimplantation
- Fibrin glue or similar hemostatic agents sprayed on cut surface

## Hepatic Vein Reconstruction: Principles

- Main reason for ex vivo resection: extensive IVC or HV involvement
- Three main HVs and major branches relatively thick-walled
- Straightforward to reconstruct even several centimeters from IVC
- For transections close to IVC: trim parenchyma for direct reimplantation

## Figure 124.19: Complex HV Reconstruction

- Two of three RHV branches joined together
- Implanted into reversed portal vein bifurcation from patient's hilum
- Transverse portion of left portal vein added to reach IVC without tension
- Cryopreserved femoral vein graft extends segment VI vein to IVC

## Figure 124.20: Prepared Autograft Diagram

- Multiple hepatic veins reconstructed with extension grafts
- Reimplantation similar to living-donor right liver graft
- Venous outflow restored before implantation

## Figure 124.21: Reimplanted Liver

- Extension graft visible
- RHV branches reimplanted
- Segment 6 vein reconstructed
- HA visible
- Demonstrates complexity of reconstruction achievable

## Venous Graft Considerations

- Grafts kept as short as possible
- Care to prevent kinking
- HV-graft anastomosis performed first
- Graft then reimplanted into IVC
- Alternative: rotate liver remnant on inflow pedicle to bring HV directly to caval graft

## IVC Reconstruction Options

- Resected IVC replaced with autologous vein or prosthetic graft
- Autologous vein superior for infection and thrombosis resistance
- Long segment replacement may require prosthetic
- Salvage native IVC portion and move superiorly for HV reimplantation
- Ringed 19-mm Gore-Tex tube graft for composite or complete replacement

## Reimplantation Sequence

- Similar to reduced-size LT or LDLT
- Suprahepatic IVC anastomosis performed first
- Artificial venous graft shortened to prevent kinking
- Back wall of infrahepatic IVC completed
- PV flushed with 500mL cold 5% albumin, vented through infrahepatic cava

## Reperfusion and Hemostasis

- Infrahepatic IVC anastomosis completed
- Cold rinse washes high-potassium UW solution out before reperfusion
- Portal limb of bypass clamped and removed
- PV anastomosis performed
- Suprahepatic IVC clamp removed, liver back-perfuses through HVs

## Arterial and Biliary Reconstruction

- Major bleeding controlled before portal reperfusion
- PV clamp removed, liver reperfused
- Cut surface bleeding controlled
- Patient taken off veno-venous bypass
- Arterial anastomosis performed
- Total warm ischemic time: 20-40 minutes

## Biliary Anastomosis

- Duct-to-duct anastomosis preferred in recent experience
- Earlier cases: Roux-en-Y choledochojejunostomy
- Duct-to-duct mirrors right lobe LDLT experience
- Stapled ends can be resected at reimplantation to avoid bile leakage

## Postoperative Course: Immediate Care

- Similar to major liver resection or liver transplantation
- Enhanced recovery protocol
- Step-down unit or ICU admission
- Ultrasound with Doppler or CT with contrast on postoperative day 1
- Assess liver blood flow

## Postoperative Laboratory Findings

- Day 1 transaminases: 200-1000 IU/L (standard)
- Return to near normal in 1 week
- Hyperbilirubinemia and coagulopathy (higher INR) common
- Varies inversely with size of liver remnant
- Hyperbilirubinemia alone not concerning if other markers improving

## Markers of Graft Function

- Early sign: return of lactate to baseline in 12-24 hours
- Maintenance of PT/INR suggests recovery of liver function
- Vitamin K and/or FFP may be needed first few days
- Target INR &lt;2

## Metabolic Considerations

- Hypophosphatemia between postoperative days 1-3
- Indicates liver regeneration
- May be profound, requiring constant IV replacement
- Expected part of recovery

## Anticoagulation Protocol

- Low-dose IV heparin (500 U/hr) perioperatively
- Hematocrit maintained between 30% and 35%
- Prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin for 30 days
- Low-dose aspirin for life in patients with artificial caval grafts
- Postoperative imaging to rule out early thrombosis

## Vascular Complications

- HA or PV thrombosis and stenosis can occur
- Suspect with sudden rise in liver enzymes (especially ALT)
- Ultrasound Doppler or urgent CT angiography with low threshold
- Full-dose anticoagulation if thrombosis occurs (&gt;1 week from surgery)
- Balloon angioplasty or endovascular stents for venous anastomotic stenosis

## Graft and IVC Complications

- Dacron IVC graft compression by regenerated liver reported
- Presents as acute Budd-Chiari syndrome
- Endovascular stent placement resolves symptoms
- Dacron tends to sclerose and occlude (usually asymptomatic due to collaterals)
- Ringed PTFE grafts currently preferred; sclerosis not encountered

## Biliary Complications

- Biliary strictures can occur with duct-to-duct anastomosis
- Approach with ERCP/PTC stent or balloon dilation
- Standard management as for any biliary anastomotic stricture

## Graft Infection

- Potential complication of these procedures
- Perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis important
- Avoiding enteric opening (choledochocholedochostomy vs choledochoenterostomy) may reduce risk
- PTFE graft-associated sepsis rarely reported in LDLT literature

## Current Role of Ex Vivo Liver Resection

- Extensive procedure in advanced malignancies: role open for discussion
- Three decades since first description, few surgeons have attempted
- Largest series from Pichlmayr's group: only 22 patients
- Major reason: in situ and ante situm techniques applicable to majority

## Why Ex Vivo Remains Rare

- Requires surgeon familiar with advanced liver resection AND liver transplantation
- Restricts procedure to relatively few individuals
- Many candidates deemed unresectable by competent surgeons and not referred
- High risk/benefit ratio
- Most literature: case reports describing technique
- Long-term follow-up often unavailable

## Outcomes: Perioperative Mortality

- Well-selected patients: perioperative mortality 10-30%
- In situ or ante situm with vascular reconstruction: 30-day mortality ≤10%
- Azoulay et al.: 90-day mortality 19.5%
- Recent ante situm series for HCC: 4% 90-day mortality
- Previous ante situm studies: 11-20% 90-day mortality

## Outcomes: Long-Term Survival

- Best 5-year survival for ex vivo malignancy: 15-30%
- Azoulay cohort: overall 5-year survival 30.4%
- Oldhafer's series: colorectal metastases median survival 21 months
- Occasional long-term survivors:
  - Cholangiocarcinoma patient disease-free at 3.5 years
  - HCC patient disease-free &gt;5 years

## The Value of Ex Vivo Capability

- Many patients benefit simply by being considered for ex vivo resection
- Qualified surgeon may realize resection possible with less aggressive technique
- In situ cold perfusion or standard vascular reconstruction may suffice
- Ex vivo consideration expands boundaries of what is deemed resectable

## Future Perspectives

- Liver surgery constantly evolving
- What is questionable today may become mainstream tomorrow
- Standard liver resection for malignancy was once considered bordering on lunacy
- Improvements in surgical technique and perioperative care transformed outcomes
- Advances in adjuvant oncologic therapies may further improve results

## Summary: Indications by Technique

- **In situ hypothermic perfusion**: Most straightforward theoretically; for tumors involving IVC/HV requiring vascular exclusion &gt;1 hour
- **Ante situm**: Better access to IVC-HV junction; no biliary/arterial reconstruction needed; for combined IVC-HV reconstruction
- **Ex vivo**: Complex HV and hilar involvement; acute Budd-Chiari; complete exteriorization for ideal exposure

## Summary: Key Technical Points

- Preoperative 3D imaging and volume assessment essential
- Veno-venous bypass often unnecessary with modern techniques
- Cold perfusion with UW or HTK solution
- Minimize warm ischemia, flush preservation solution before reperfusion
- Meticulous vascular reconstruction without time pressure on back table
- Temperature and hemodynamic management critical

## Summary: Patient Selection

- Highly selected patients in specialized centers
- Normal liver function or compensated disease preferred
- CCI &lt;3, tumor &lt;10 cm, creatinine &lt;1.3 mg/dL
- Adequate future liver remnant (&gt;40% if complex reconstruction)
- No extrahepatic disease

## Conclusion

- Ex vivo and in situ hypothermic hepatic resection represent the extreme frontier of liver surgery
- Require expertise in both hepatic resection and liver transplantation
- Appropriate for select patients with otherwise unresectable tumors
- Technique selection should minimize complexity while achieving oncologic goals
- Continued evolution of these techniques may expand their role in the future
